questions.q: Metro/Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) working is governed by which set of documents?
options: Only the train timetable
The organisation's Rule Book / General & Subsidiary Rules, Operating Procedures and Safety Manuals
The station duty roster alone
Instructions pasted on the notice board
questions.explain: In simple words: the Rule Book, G&SR, operating procedures and safety manuals together govern how the railway is run.

questions.q: Independent safety oversight for opening new metro/Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) sections is through whom?
options: The station master
The train operator
The Commissioner of Metro Railway Safety (CMRS)
The Operations Control Centre (OCC) duty officer alone
questions.explain: New sections are opened only under the approved safety regime, with the Commissioner of Metro Railway Safety (CMRS) giving independent safety oversight.

questions.q: In any conflict, what is the correct golden hierarchy of priorities?
options: Safety of life > safety of property > service and punctuality
Punctuality > safety of life > property
Property > life > punctuality
Punctuality first, safety if time permits
questions.explain: Life always comes first, then property, and only then punctuality — this order never changes.

questions.q: A senior officer orders an action you believe is unsafe. What must you do?
options: Obey because the officer is senior
Do it slowly so it becomes safe
Ask a passenger to decide
Refuse the unsafe act and report it through the proper channel
questions.explain: No instruction from anyone can authorise an unsafe act; staff must refuse and report it properly.

questions.q: Who may perform safety-critical tasks such as driving, controlling or shunting?
options: Any staff member on duty
Only the most senior staff, trained or not
Only trained, examined, medically fit and authorised staff
Contract staff without examination
questions.explain: Safety-critical work needs all four: training, examination, medical fitness and formal authorisation.

questions.q: A staff member's competency for a safety-critical task has lapsed. What is the rule?
options: They must not perform safety-critical duty until competency is renewed
They may work if a colleague watches
They may work only at night
They may work for one more month
questions.explain: Lapsed competency means no safety-critical duty — there is no grace period.

questions.q: A train may move only when which conditions are met?
options: The platform is empty
The driver feels confident
The previous train has left the depot
Movement authority exists, the route is proved and locked, and speed is at or below the permitted limit
questions.explain: Authority, a proved and locked route, and permitted speed — all three, every time.

questions.q: In degraded working, from where can a movement authority come?
options: From a passenger's request
From an Operations Control Centre (OCC) instruction, when signalling cannot give a movement authority
From the station announcer
It is never needed in degraded working
questions.explain: When the signalling system cannot give the authority, Operations Control Centre (OCC) authorises movement under degraded-working rules.

questions.q: What does PSR stand for in train operation?
options: Platform Safety Rule
Permanent Speed Restriction
Passenger Service Regulation
Power Supply Restriction
questions.explain: A PSR is a fixed speed limit for a section, built into the normal rules for that location.

questions.q: A caution order mainly informs the operator about what?
options: Salary and leave details
Canteen timings
Temporary speed restrictions and special conditions on the route
The next day's roster
questions.explain: Caution orders bridge the gap between the printed timetable and today's real track conditions, including TSRs.

questions.q: An operator notices an unusual sound and a possible track defect. What is the duty?
options: Report it immediately — reporting an abnormality is a duty, not a choice
Note it and report at the end of the month
Ignore it if the train is running fine
Tell only the next operator informally
questions.explain: Every abnormality — defect, obstruction, smoke, trespasser — must be reported at once.

questions.q: What is the absolute rule about passing a signal or movement-authority limit at danger?
options: Pass slowly if the track looks clear
Pass if running late
Pass after blowing the whistle
Never pass it; if in doubt, stop
questions.explain: Never pass a signal/MA limit at danger. When in doubt, stop — nobody is punished for stopping safely.

questions.q: What are the four checks behind safe train movement, as taught by the highway example?
options: Fuel, lights, horn and mirrors
Ticket, roster, uniform and radio
Authority, safe speed, proved route and working brakes
Weather, crowd, time and distance
questions.explain: Like a good road driver: green light (authority), speed limit, clear lane (proved route) and tested brakes.

questions.q: A train has failed in a section. What must happen before any detraining of passengers?
options: Inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), secure the train and protect it as per rules
Open all doors immediately
Ask passengers to walk to the next station at once
Switch off the radio to save battery
questions.explain: Protection comes before detraining: inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), secure the train, protect as per rules.

questions.q: How are shunting and depot movements controlled?
options: At normal line speed
By whichever staff member is free
Without any communication to save time
Under separate low-speed rules, with a designated shunter in charge and continuous communication
questions.explain: Depot and shunting moves are slow, led by a named shunter, with communication maintained throughout.

questions.q: What is the correct order of actions on finding the line ahead obstructed?
options: Inform Operations Control Centre (OCC), keep moving slowly, then stop
Stop the train, protect the line, then inform Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Pass carefully, then note it in the report
Blow the whistle continuously and proceed
questions.explain: Stop — Protect — Inform. Passing 'carefully' past an obstruction is how collisions happen.

questions.q: Classical protection of an obstructed line in an emergency uses what?
options: Headlights only
Detonators/fog signals and hand danger signals placed at prescribed distances, with information to control
Whistling only
A phone call to the depot
questions.explain: Audible detonators warn an approaching driver even in fog, backed by hand danger signals.

questions.q: Before a train starts, which test confirms the braking system works through the train?
options: The horn test
The headlight test
The brake continuity test
The door chime test
questions.explain: Brake continuity proves the brakes respond along the whole train, not just in the driving cab.

questions.q: A train operator receives an instruction but is unsure whether it is safe. The best action is:
options: Stop, secure the train and seek clarification from Operations Control Centre (OCC)
Guess and proceed
Ask a passenger
Proceed at full speed to clear the section
questions.explain: 'When in doubt, stop and ask' is the universal safe answer in operations.

questions.q: Scenario: You see a trespasser walking on the track ahead. Your first duty is to:
options: Ignore him as he will move away
Slow down slightly and continue
Report it after reaching the destination
Take action to stop/protect as required and report it to Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately
questions.explain: A trespasser is an abnormality affecting safe movement — protect and report at once, do not just carry on.

questions.q: Scenario: A temporary speed restriction is in force but you are running 10 minutes late. You should:
options: Ignore the restriction to make up time
Exceed it slightly where the track looks straight
Obey the restriction exactly; time is never recovered by breaking a restriction
Follow it only if Operations Control Centre (OCC) reminds you
questions.explain: PSR, TSR and caution orders must be obeyed exactly — punctuality never outranks safety.

questions.q: Which of these is a look-out duty connected with safe train movement?
options: Watching the line ahead for obstructions, defects and persons and reporting them
Watching passenger luggage
Watching the advertisement boards
Watching the clock only
questions.explain: The operator's eyes are a safety device: defects, obstructions and trespassers must be spotted and reported.

questions.q: Why are safety rules described as 'written in the memory of past accidents'?
options: Because rules are very old
Because rules are hard to memorise
Because accidents are celebrated
Because most rules exist as a result of someone being hurt when the rule was not followed
questions.explain: Every rule carries a lesson from a past accident — that is why shortcuts with rules are so dangerous.

questions.q: In degraded working, an Operations Control Centre (OCC) instruction authorising movement must be treated as:
options: A casual suggestion
A formal movement authority, to be followed exactly within its limits
Valid for the whole day
Transferable to any other train
questions.explain: An Operations Control Centre (OCC) degraded-working instruction is a real authority with defined limits — follow it exactly, nothing beyond it.

questions.q: Which statement about speed on a section is correct?
options: A train may exceed the limit in automatic mode
A train must run at or below the permitted speed for that section and that mode of operation
Speed limits apply only in tunnels
Speed limits are advisory only
questions.explain: The permitted speed depends on both the section and the operating mode, and it is a ceiling, not a target.

questions.q: What does 'route proved and locked' mean for safe movement?
options: The driver has memorised the route
The route is painted on the platform
The path is set, verified and locked so no conflicting movement can be given over it
All signals on the route are green forever
questions.explain: Proving and locking guarantees your train's path cannot be taken away or crossed by another movement.

questions.q: Scenario: Smoke is seen coming from the track area ahead. The operator should:
options: Stop as required, protect the train and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately
Speed up to pass the smoke quickly
Open the doors so passengers can see
Wait until the next station to mention it
questions.explain: Smoke is an abnormality — stop/protect and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) at once; never run into an unknown hazard.

questions.q: Which priority is correct when a service decision conflicts with a safety rule?
options: Service wins during peak hours
The senior officer present decides freely
Whichever is cheaper wins
The safety rule wins, even if the service is delayed or suspended
questions.explain: Safety of life sits above property and punctuality — a delay is always acceptable, an unsafe act never is.

questions.q: What must an operator do with a caution order received for the trip?
options: File it without reading
Follow only the first restriction
Read it, understand the restrictions and special conditions, and obey them on that trip
Pass it to a passenger for safekeeping
questions.explain: A caution order is useless unread — it carries today's TSRs and special conditions for your exact route.

questions.q: Shunting movements are kept safe mainly by which combination?
options: Low speed, a designated shunter in charge and continuous communication
High speed to finish quickly
Hand signals from passengers
One staff member working alone silently
questions.explain: Slow speed plus a named person in charge plus constant communication is the shunting safety formula.

questions.q: If a signal fails and no movement authority can be obtained, the train should:
options: Proceed on the driver's judgement
Reverse to the previous station on its own
Follow the train ahead closely
Remain stopped and act only on Operations Control Centre (OCC) instructions under degraded-working rules
questions.explain: No authority means no movement — degraded working starts only with Operations Control Centre (OCC)'s formal instruction.

questions.q: Which of these staff may be given a safety-critical duty?
options: A new recruit on his first day, unsupervised
A trained, examined, medically fit and authorised staff member whose competency is current
A staff member whose medical has expired
A volunteer from the public
questions.explain: All four conditions — trained, examined, medically fit, authorised — plus current competency.

questions.q: What is the correct response to an order that conflicts with the Rule Book?
options: Carry it out and complain later
Do not carry it out; refuse the unsafe act and report through the proper channel
Carry it out only in writing
Ask another junior staff to do it
questions.explain: The Rule Book cannot be overridden by any individual's order; refusal plus reporting is the protected course.

questions.q: A failed train must be 'secured' before protection. Securing mainly means:
options: Locking the passenger doors only
Switching off the lights
Making sure the train cannot move — brakes applied and the train held safely
Removing the operator from the cab
questions.explain: A secured train cannot roll or move unexpectedly while staff protect it and plan the next step.

questions.q: Why must restrictions like PSR and TSR be obeyed 'exactly', not approximately?
options: Because they are calculated for the actual condition of that section of track
Because Operations Control Centre (OCC) checks the speedometer only
Because passengers complain otherwise
Because the timetable says so
questions.explain: A restriction reflects a real physical limit — exceeding it even slightly removes the safety margin.

questions.q: Which document would a supervisor check to confirm the operating rules for a task?
options: The canteen menu
The passenger feedback register
The advertising contract
The Rule Book / General & Subsidiary Rules and the relevant Operating Procedures
questions.explain: Rules live in the Rule Book/G&SR, operating procedures and safety manuals — not in habit or hearsay.

questions.q: Scenario: Your train is held at a signal showing danger, but the platform behind is crowded and pressure is building. You should:
options: Pass the signal slowly to clear the platform
Ask passengers to push the train
Stay stopped until a proper authority is given; crowding never justifies passing danger
Open doors and let passengers walk along the track
questions.explain: A danger signal is absolute. Crowd pressure is managed by station staff and Operations Control Centre (OCC), never by passing danger.

questions.q: The safety regime under which metro railways operate includes which legal framework, as per the book?
options: The Metro Railways (Operation and Maintenance) Act framework
The Motor Vehicles Act
The Shops and Establishments Act
The Factories Act alone
questions.explain: Metro/Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) working is framed under the Metro Railways (O&M) Act framework and its approved safety regime.

questions.q: Which of the following is part of protecting a failed train?
options: Hiding the failure to avoid paperwork
Letting the next train find out itself
Switching off all communication
Informing Operations Control Centre (OCC) so following movements can be stopped or controlled
questions.explain: Protection is practical: Operations Control Centre (OCC) must know at once so no other train is sent into danger.

questions.q: An operator who proceeds unsafely instead of stopping will face what, as per the book's key point?
options: A reward for saving time
People are punished for proceeding unsafely; no one is punished for stopping safely
Nothing, if no accident happens
A small fine only
questions.explain: The culture protects the safe stop — the unsafe proceed is what attracts punishment, accident or not.

questions.q: In Absolute Block System working, the basic rule that keeps trains safe is:
options: Two trains may follow each other closely in the same section
Only one train is allowed in a block section at a time, and the next train enters only after the section is cleared
Trains run purely on time interval
The driver proceeds on sight at full speed
questions.explain: Absolute Block means one train, one block section. The section must be proved clear and 'line clear' obtained before the next train is allowed in — this separation is the oldest and strongest protection against rear-end and head-on collisions.

questions.q: A written Caution Order is handed to a train driver mainly so that he:
options: Knows his duty roster for the week
Is informed in writing of speed restrictions and unusual conditions ahead on the route
Can skip the brake test
Is excused from obeying signals
questions.explain: A Caution Order puts temporary speed restrictions, worksites and unusual conditions in writing before the driver. Verbal information can be forgotten or misheard — the written order travels with the driver and can be re-read.

questions.q: Before a train is allowed to enter a block section, the station ahead must grant 'line clear'. Line clear is granted only after:
options: The previous train has been seen by passengers
It is confirmed that the block section is free and the line is clear up to the required point
The driver sounds the horn twice
The timetable says the train is due
questions.explain: Line clear is a formal confirmation, not a formality: the section must actually be free of the previous train and obstructions before the next movement authority is given.

questions.q: During dense fog, the safest combination for train movement is:
options: Normal speed with headlight on full
Reduced speed as prescribed, fog signals/detonators and fog-safe devices used, and extra vigilance by the crew
Depend only on the horn
Cancel every train on the network
questions.explain: Fog destroys the driver's main sense — sight. Speed is cut so the train can stop within the visible distance, and fog signals, detonators and fog-safe devices replace the missing visual information.

questions.q: A train parts into two portions while running (train parting). The driver's FIRST duties are to:
options: Speed up to rejoin the portions
Stop and secure both portions, protect the line as per rules and inform Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately
Leave the rear portion and continue to the next station silently
Ask passengers to push the rear portion
questions.explain: A parted train leaves an unprotected portion standing on the line — a collision waiting to happen. Both portions are secured, the line is protected, and Operations Control Centre (OCC) is informed at once so no other train is sent into the section.
